articles.title: Internal revolt erupts as Trump appointee enrages Wall Street: 'Not confident'
articles.description: One of President Donald Trump's most scrutinized appointees faces an internal revolt after his first major address to the press imploded . Multiple Fed officials are fuming that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh enraged Wall Street Wednesday with his claim that there was no reason to raise short-term interest rates, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday. Three Federal Reserve policymakers have publicly challenged Warsh's decision to hold rates steady, signaling mounting internal pressure for action on inflation, according to the report. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari dissented from the committee's decision to maintain rates at 3.5% to 3.75%, voting instead for an increase. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan joined them in the dissent. In separate statements Friday morning, Hammack and Kashkari explained their positions. Hammack expressed concern that inflation, which has remained above 2 percent for more than five years, will not return to target without Fed action. "I am not confident it will return to our objective on its own," she said. Kashkari warned that accelerated price increases could continue if the Fed doesn't tighten policy. He indicated willingness to support a series of rate increases to prevent inflation from becoming entrenched. "A potential series of small policy moves would be better than waiting and eventually concluding that even bolder actions were necessary," he said. The three dissents represent a significant internal challenge to Warsh's leadership after just months on the job. The 12-member policy committee voted 9-3 to hold rates steady Wednesday, with the Journal pointing it was the first time since 2016 that three officials have dissented in the same direction. According to the Journal, Kashkari's dissent "caught many off guard," noting that, "as recently as March, he had projected that the Fed might need to bring rates lower this year, not higher, to protect a job market that at the time appeared to be weakening."

articles.title: Govt will resolve your issues and ensure your protection, Naqvi tells traders from KP and Balochistan
articles.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has met a delegation of traders and industrialists from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan and assured them that the government would employ all available resources to resolve their issues and ensure their protection, the interior ministry said on Friday. In a statement on X, the ministry said representatives from all chambers of commerce spoke about the security situation in their respective provinces and the challenges they were facing. For his part, Naqvi briefed the delegation on the overall security situation in the country, particularly in KP and Balochistan, and the steps taken by the government in this regard, the statement added. “He assured the business community of complete cooperation,” it stated, further quoting Naqvi as saying: “The government will employ all available resources to resolve the issues of traders and industrialists and ensure their protection.” He further said that he would soon visit Peshawar and Quetta and hold detailed meetings with the business community in the presence of senior government officials and representatives so that “a permanent and practical solution” for the challenges being faced by traders and industrialists could be worked out. He further said, “The private sector plays a key role in stabilising the country’s economy. Pakistan’s progress lies in the progress of the business community. The government is with you and we will resolve all your legitimate issues.” Naqvi’s meeting with members of the business community takes place against the backdrop of security challenges in KP and Balochistan. A monthly security assessment released in early June by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) said that after two consecutive months of improvement, Pakistan’s security situation deteriorated sharply in May, driven primarily by escalating terrorist violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Earlier this month, security forces and law enforcement personnel jointly launched Operation Shaban in Balochistan in retaliation for a deadly attack on a police post at the Mangi Dam pumping station in Ziarat on July 6. During that assault, armed attackers kidnapped and killed 27 police officers . Later, security forces also launched Operation Al-Azm in the province after a shooting on a Karachi-bound coach coming from Quetta claimed three lives and injured five others last week. More recently, in KP, nine policemen, including a deputy superintendent of police, were martyred and 28 others injured after terrorists attacked the Khazina Banda checkpost in Hangu district late on Wednesday. A statement issued by KP Inspector General Zulfiqar Hameed said that the checkpost was attacked by Fitna-al-Khawarij , a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. Also on Wednesday, a policeman was martyred and four terrorists were killed during an operation in Swat’s Matta tehsil. On July 24, terrorists also attempted to breach a joint police checkpost’s perimeter in Tank, and according to ISPR, the attempt was “swiftly and decisively foiled” by security forces, who eliminated 12 terrorists. On Thursday, Naqvi had held a meeting with President Asif Ali Zardari, during which both reviewed the country’s overall law and order situation, with particular focus on the security situation in KP and Balochistan. The interior minister had briefed the president on the prevailing law and order situation in the two provinces, as well as the ongoing measures being taken to combat terrorism.

articles.title: Trump administration stops work on Great Lakes Asian carp project near Joliet
articles.description:
Gov. JB Pritzker is calling on the Trump administration to immediately reverse a work stoppage on an embattled project needed to keep invasive Asian carp out of the Great Lakes near Joliet.

Contractors at the Brandon Road Interbasin Project received a work stoppage order on July 24 stating the project is under administrative review, despite about $2 million worth of material already on site. Work was slated to begin this week, with shaft drilling scheduled for September. Jobsite trailers were also already set up at the project, according to Will County officials.

"Under my administration, Illinois has spearheaded this project to protect the entire Great Lakes region. Yet, the Trump Administration repeatedly throws up roadblocks and has now ordered work to stop altogether with no explanations,” Pritzker said Thursday. “The Great Lakes provide drinking water to more than 40 million people and support a $52 billion regional economy. It's time for the Trump Administration to uphold the federal government’s obligations, stop playing political games, and move this project forward.”

The $1.15 billion project in the Des Plaines River near Joliet is seen as a crucial way to stop invasive Asian carp from entering the Great Lakes. Without a barrier, the carp could wreak havoc on the $20 billion fishing and boating industries and upend the freshwater ecosystem, experts say. The species already has made it into the Illinois River from the Mississippi River. Fishermen contracted by the state of Illinois have removed more than 78 million pounds of invasive carp from waterways.

There have been several delays to the project, including a pause in December for another administrative review. President Donald Trump in March said "only Trump" could save the Great Lakes from Asian carp and urged governors to "join in on the fight." Those words on social media came after he met with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, prompting both Pritzker and Sen. Dick Durbin to demand Trump lift the review and release federal funds on the Joliet project.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in April instead announced that it would put Michigan officials in charge of the $1.15 billion barrier designed to keep the invasive carp from reaching the Great Lakes — moving from the Rock Island district to its Detroit District.

Both sides engaged in a war of words in April, with Pritzker calling the move a “political stunt” and warning that Illinois would explore legal action if the Trump administration broke legally-binding agreements. In announcing the move, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Adam Telle accused Illinois of being an “unreliable partner, delinquent on its payments and real estate commitments,” a claim that Pritzker denied.

The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said it first learned of the work stoppage through contractors — and followed through on a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on Thursday, with the work stoppage confirmed on July 28 after repeated attempts to reach their Detroit District.

Renee Snow, interim IDNR director, wrote in a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers that she wants an “immediate” meeting to “substantiate the work stoppage and remedy project cost, schedule, and partnership impacts.”

Snow wrote that the breakdown in communication is inconsistent with procedures established under a jointly negotiated plan that guided the project.

Gary G. Perinar III, president of Carpenters Local 174 in Joliet, told the Sun-Times the project delays “not only endanger the safety of the Great Lakes but also negatively affect the working men and women who have supported this project locally.”

“This project needs to happen,” Perinar III said. “...Our members stand by eagerly awaiting the opportunity to get the job done building and strengthening our communities.”

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

articles.title: Court lets Trump admin force some terminally ill patients to work for health care
articles.description: A federal judge on Thursday denied a request by more than two dozen Democratic states to halt a Trump administration policy announced last month that would require Medicaid recipients with terminal diseases to prove they are too sick to work in order to be exempt from new work requirements that go into effect this coming January. While introducing over $1 trillion in tax cuts for the wealthiest 1% of Americans, last year’s massive GOP tax and budget bill also imposed new 80-hour-per-month work requirements that states must implement for Medicaid expansion recipients, who receive government-subsidized insurance coverage at or below 138% of the poverty line. The law specified that those who are “medically frail or otherwise have special medical needs” are excluded from the work requirement, and specifically listed people with a “serious or complex medical condition.” But it remained unclear what exact conditions met these criteria. Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) introduced a new rule stating that even if a person receives a terminal diagnosis for a disease like cancer, HIV/AIDS, or Parkinson’s, that is still not enough for them to be exempt from the work requirements. Beginning on January 1, 2028, it says they must also demonstrate to states that their condition “significantly impairs” their ability to meet the work requirement. Democratic attorneys general in 25 states and the District of Columbia filed a preliminary injunction over the rule late last month, arguing that CMS had rewritten the law to introduce a vague and needlessly restrictive new hurdle that vulnerable people will face in obtaining desperately needed care. “This is one of those cases where it’s really hard to overstate how dire the consequences could be,” North Carolina’s Democratic attorney general, Jeff Jackson, told Politico . “You’re going to have 50 states doing 50 different things, and we’re all going to have to create a whole new bureaucracy... You are talking about a lot more paperwork, more evaluations, more doctor visits, and a lot more work for doctors themselves.” The Democratic AGs argued that implementation of the work requirements should be paused because they lacked the staff or capacity to meet the timeline set by CMS, which requires states to communicate to enrollees how they’ll be affected by the changes by the end of August. US District Judge Richard Stearns on Thursday denied their initial request to immediately halt the implementation of the requirements while the lawsuit proceeds, but also did not rule on the lawsuit’s merits, which are scheduled to be decided before the requirements go into effect on January 1. Several medical associations, including the American Medical Association , the American College of Physicians , and the American Academy of Pediatrics , have come out against the rule, arguing that it would have dire consequences for people who suffer from severe illness. “One of the most significant factors in whether someone survives a cancer diagnosis is whether they have health insurance coverage,” Lisa Lacasse, president of the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, explained in June. “The new restrictions link the definition of medical frailty to a person’s ability to work,” she continued. “This would mean cancer patients and survivors who are suffering from debilitating side effects of the disease or treatment would have to officially prove they can’t work, in a process that is likely to be difficult and take a long time.” The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has projected that over the coming decade, changes to healthcare policy introduced by Republicans would increase the number of uninsured Americans by about 11.8 million. Around 5.7 million of them are projected to be Medicaid recipients who either do not meet the 80-hour work requirement or are otherwise eligible but tripped up by one of the newly imposed paperwork hurdles. Taya Graham and Stephen Janis argued earlier this week in a piece for The Real News Network that eligible people losing coverage is not an unfortunate side effect of the law, but a goal of the Republicans who passed it, who sought a way to thin the ranks of those who qualify for Medicaid without having to take the politically unpopular step of actually clawing back benefits. They wrote that what has happened to recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program ( SNAP ) illustrates how burdensome these new requirements may become. As The New York Times reported earlier this month, in Arizona, 440,000 people have already been dropped from SNAP after it enacted a formidable regime of paperwork for low-income recipients to prove eligibility, including requiring some people with panhandling income to obtain documentation from donors who drop them a buck on the street. “If this is what people receiving SNAP benefits have been subjected to,” Graham and Janis wrote, “imagine what’s going to happen to people who will need to navigate the new [Medicaid] requirements while struggling with a debilitating or terminal illness.” Medical issues are a leading cause of bankruptcy in the US. According to one study , over 4 in 10 cancer patients over 50 had depleted all their assets within two years of diagnosis. Melanie D’Arrigo, a campaigner for single-payer healthcare in New York, said that President Donald Trump “cut cancer research, cut healthcare,” and with new Medicaid restrictions, “wants to make sure Americans continue to work as they go broke battling cancer.”
